title: Zeptojoule Microwave Calorimetry with Nanosecond Recovery in Graphene
authors: Seunghan Lee, Woochan Jung, Jayeon Kim, Dongsung T. Park, Seong Jang, Seongeun Jeon, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Jong-Chul Park, Philip Kim, Kin Chung Fong, Gil-Ho Lee
abstract: Graphene calorimeters are predicted to combine extreme energy sensitivity with rapid thermal recovery, yet experiments remain far from ideal estimates. Here, we directly calibrate a graphene Josephson-junction microwave calorimeter using nanosecond pulses and independently determine the thermal parameters of the same operating device. At 110 mK, calibrated pulse measurements yield a characteristic switching-energy scale of 18.1 meV (2.90 zJ), while time-resolved two-pulse thermometry gives an intrinsic relaxation time of 19.5 ns. Pulse-width-dependent calorimetry and bolometric thermometry show that the electronic heat capacity is 12.4 times and the electron-phonon coupling is approximately 50 times larger than ideal estimates. A thermal model using these measured parameters predicts 21.2 meV, quantitatively reproducing the observed switching response. These results identify the microscopic origin of the sensitivity gap in graphene calorimeters and establish a self-consistent calibration framework for ultrafast nanoscale thermal detectors.
summary: This paper experimentally characterizes a graphene Josephson-junction microwave calorimeter by measuring its thermal properties using nanosecond pulses. The authors determined that the electronic heat capacity and electron-phonon coupling are significantly enhanced compared to theoretical predictions. These measured parameters allow for the construction of a self-consistent thermal model, resolving discrepancies in the calorimeter's energy sensitivity.
main_problem: To overcome the trade-off in graphene calorimeters between high energy sensitivity and slow thermal recovery, and to establish a self-consistent calibration framework for ultrafast nanoscale thermal detectors.
main_result: The study successfully calibrated the calorimeter, finding that the electronic heat capacity and electron-phonon coupling are significantly larger than ideal estimates, which allows for a quantitative thermal model reproducing the observed switching response.
method: The authors used direct calibration via nanosecond microwave pulses and time-resolved two-pulse thermometry to measure thermal parameters.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Graphene Josephson-junction (GJJ) microwave calorimeter operating at 110 mK. The thermal dynamics are governed by a heat balance equation involving electronic heat capacity ($C_e$) and electron-phonon coupling ($\Sigma$).
key_observables: Characteristic switching-energy scale ($E_{	ext{thres}}$), intrinsic relaxation time ($	au_{	ext{th}}$), electronic heat capacity ($C_e$), and electron–phonon coupling.
important_parameters: Measured values include $E_{	ext{thres}} = 18.1 	ext{ meV}$ and $	au_{	ext{th}} = 19.5 	ext{ ns}$. The extracted $C_e$ is $12.4$ times and the coupling is $\approx 50$ times larger than ideal estimates.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the measured parameters can be used in a self-consistent thermal model to explain the observed switching response, though the authors note that the measured parameters might be upper bounds.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the device structure and detection principle using SEM and schematic diagrams. Figure 2 details the pulse-based calibration, showing the temporal profile of the microwave pulse and the dependence of detection efficiency on absorbed energy.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the challenge of graphene calorimeters, then details the experimental setup and measurement techniques (pulse calibration, two-pulse thermometry). It presents the quantitative results showing the measured thermal parameters, validates these parameters using a thermal model, and concludes by establishing a self-consistent calibration framework.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed, quantitative experimental characterization of thermal energy dissipation in a 2D material system, which is crucial for understanding non-equilibrium thermodynamics in nanoscale quantum devices.
